title: Pitkin Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Pitkin wells have a 40 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $8,600-$16,000.
h1: Private Well Information for Pitkin, Colorado
intro_html:
For properties near Pitkin, the well records show a shallow typical well but a mountain-groundwater setting that still needs careful review. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median completed depth is 40 feet, and the middle half runs from 30 to 78 feet. Reported production is also strong where data is available: the median pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for planning, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. Most permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, and only 26 wells report a static water level. Before buying land, compare nearby well permits, confirm the intended use, and have a driller evaluate access, casing, grout, pump equipment, and the proposed septic and building sites.

sections.heading: Pitkin well depths reflect shallow mountain groundwater
sections.html:
Among 289 wells reporting total depth, the median is 40 feet. The middle half falls between 30 and 78 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 190 feet. The depth mix shows why local records matter: 79% are under 100 feet, 16% are 100-300 feet, 4% are 300-600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 690 feet.

For a drilling bid, the 40-foot median is a useful starting point, not a promised target. Fractured granite and gneiss can change quickly over short distances. A nearby shallow well may not predict the depth on your lot, especially if the parcel sits on a different fracture zone or has difficult access.

sections.heading: What Pitkin wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Only 99 permitted wells report a pump yield, so the yield statistics do not describe every constructed well. In that reporting group, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-three percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, 22% report 5-15 gallons per minute, and 5% report 1-5 gallons per minute. None report under 1 gallon per minute.

This is a favorable local production record, but it is not a guarantee of a new well's performance. A driller should explain the proposed test, recovery, pump setting, storage, and any seasonal limitations. Most permits are for domestic or household use, and the 35-gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit still applies where an exempt well is authorized.

sections.heading: Pitkin water levels are shallow, but the trend is limited
sections.html:
Just 26 wells in the records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is small. Those wells have a median depth to water of 12 feet, with the middle half from 6 to 22 feet. That suggests groundwater is often relatively shallow in the reported locations, but it should not be treated as a parcel-specific measurement.

The permit history does not provide enough reported static levels to establish a reliable decline or rise by decade. Ask for a current measurement from any existing well and compare it with the well permit and construction report. A shallow water level can reduce pumping lift, but it also makes proper casing, grout, surface drainage, and sanitary protection important.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Pitkin, and how old are the records
sections.html:
The records include 381 permitted wells within 5 miles of Pitkin, with 291 recorded as constructed and 289 reporting a total depth. Bob Williams Drilling Co., listed as Williams, Robert F., appears most often, with 224 records. Williams Drilling Co Inc., listed as Williams, Frank, appears in 11, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears in 9.

Permit activity spans several decades: 2 permits in the 1950s, 58 in the 1970s, 63 in the 1980s, 62 in the 1990s, 79 in the 2000s, 36 in the 2010s, and 26 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Treat older records as useful context, then verify current licensing, insurance, references, and the scope of any new drilling proposal.

sections.heading: A Pitkin well budget starts with the bedrock
sections.html:
Ground in this area is fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The drilling model uses a typical rate of $65-$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 40 feet, the drilled hole alone works out to about $2,600-$4,000.

A finished water system costs more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the modeled total at the median depth is about $8,600-$16,000. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, longer utility runs, and site constraints can change the bid. Ask each driller to separate drilling, casing, grout, testing, pump equipment, trenching, and electrical so competing proposals can be compared.

sections.heading: Checks for contamination, low yield, and building conflicts
sections.html:
Local environmental review deserves attention. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 865 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to review land history, nearby mine workings, and water-quality testing before closing.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock even though the reported yield records are generally strong. Confirm the well location, casing and grout, pump test results, and laboratory water tests. Also keep the well, septic system, access drive, and building envelope coordinated. A good water source does not solve an unsuitable septic or building site.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Pitkin: use the records before committing
sections.html:
Start with the well permits around the specific parcel, not only the area median. Compare depths, reported yields, static levels, construction details, and the stated use. Nearby Garfield, Maysville, Almont, Gunnison, Poncha Springs, and Buena Vista can provide broader regional context, but the most useful comparisons are the closest wells in similar ground.

For an existing home, make the sale contingent on a well inspection, production test, water-quality testing, and review of the permit and completion report. For vacant land, have a Colorado driller assess access and a qualified septic professional review the lot before you finalize a building plan. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask the Colorado Division of Water Resources whether an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement applies.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Pitkin, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Pitkin is 40 feet, and the middle half runs from 30 to 78 feet. Seventy-nine percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, but the 90th percentile is 190 feet and the deepest record is 690 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can make one lot differ substantially from its neighbors.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Pitkin?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 40-foot median depth, drilling the hole is modeled at about $2,600-$4,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $8,600-$16,000. Access, depth, casing, grout, and utility distance can change the final proposal.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Pitkin?
faq.a: Among the 99 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0-15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-three percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Those results are encouraging, but a new well still needs a properly documented production and recovery test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Pitkin, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Nearby mapping includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 865 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well through a qualified laboratory, review local land and mine history, and check construction details such as casing and grout before relying on the water.

faq.q: Are Pitkin wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The available records do not support a reliable decline or rise trend. Only 26 wells report static water levels; their median depth to water is 12 feet, with a middle half of 6-22 feet. For a property decision, obtain a current water-level measurement and compare it with the well's permit, completion report, and production history.
